design_detail: Systematic review with a narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis), following PRISMA: PubMed and Scopus searched from market introduction (gabapentin 1997, pregabalin 2004) to 31 March 2017, plus a hand search of reference lists; 106 articles included. The evidence is organized after Griffiths and Johnson (2006) into steps: rewarding effects in animals and humans (17 publications); clinical and epidemiological studies of abuse and dependence (14; Table 1); case reports scored by the reviewers against the six ICD-10 dependence criteria (38 publications: 36 gabapentin and 19 pregabalin case presentations; Table 2); non-fatal and fatal overdoses (37 publications; Table 3). It ends with the authors' star-rated comparison of the addictive risks of gabapentin and pregabalin with those of opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines and cannabis (Table 4).
can_establish: What the published literature up to March 2017 contained on the rewarding effects of gabapentinoids, on rates of non-medical use in people in opioid treatment, on the dependence criteria described in case reports, and on overdoses and deaths involving gabapentinoids, and that almost all published cases of behavioural dependence occurred in people with other substance use disorders.
cannot_establish: The risk of dependence among people prescribed gabapentinoids (case reports have no denominator, and the only general-population figures come from one online survey and one hospital survey of older people); whether gabapentinoids cause the deaths in which they are found (registry deaths nearly always involve other drugs); or the comparative ratings of Table 4, which rest partly on the authors' clinical expertise.

sample.recruitment: PubMed and Scopus searches with the terms listed (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 1st paragraph), from 1997 (gabapentin) or 2004 (pregabalin) to 31 March 2017, and a hand search of reference lists. The included clinical studies came mostly from opioid substitution programmes, detoxification wards and people misusing prescription opioids, plus one online survey and one hospital survey; fatality data came from case reports, poison-centre annual reports, pharmacovigilance and national post-mortem and death registers (Tables 1 and 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Eligible: articles on (i) rewarding behaviour and self-administration, (ii) clinical studies of gabapentinoid addiction, (iii) case reports of gabapentinoid addiction, (iv) overdoses, suicides and deaths. Excluded: reviews; articles unrelated to these topics; articles on gabapentinoids used to treat disorders other than addiction (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). No language restriction is stated (included articles in Norwegian, Danish and German appear in the references).
sample.demographics: Not summarized across studies; Tables 1 to 3 give each study's population.
sample.attrition: PRISMA (Figure 1, PDF p. 3, legible): 1073 records from databases and 19 from hand search; 878 after duplicates removed and screened; 709 excluded on title and abstract; 169 full texts; 63 excluded (reviews, not related to addiction, overdose, death or self-poisoning, wrong patient group, poison-centre annual reports before 2012); 106 included. No list of excluded full texts.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases and reference lists, no grey literature search (although agency reports were included), no appraisal of included studies. The clinical evidence comes mostly from people in opioid treatment, and case reports are a publication-driven selection whose missing details (54% of ICD-10 items) the authors treat as absent. Two included sources are the authors' own (Cossmann et al., 2016, the only hospital-population dependence figure; Bonnet and Scherbaum, 2016, six gabapentin cases). Only US poison-centre reports from 2012 to 2015 were considered (Table 3 footnote, PDF p. 20).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each included study used: self-report questionnaires, structured interviews (SKID-I, DSM-IV), urine or hair testing, case descriptions, post-mortem toxicology, register, poison-centre and pharmacovigilance records.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded for each study in the tables (addiction history and comorbidity). The review's central analysis separates case reports with and without a history of other substance use disorders, and notes that all clinical-study participants found to misuse or depend on gabapentinoids were dependent on at least one other substance, mostly opioids (PDF p. 4, 3.2, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: No comparator at review level, except one clinical study with a control group (people treated for non-opioid addictions; Grosshans et al., 2013) and Table 4's comparison with opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines and cannabis by star ratings.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the case reports' histories of other substance use are often unknown or incomplete.

outcomes.instruments: ICD-10 dependence criteria applied by the reviewers to case descriptions (craving, loss of control and narrowed behaviour as behavioural dependence; tolerance, withdrawal and harmful use as physical dependence); prevalence of non-medical use in clinical studies; overdose blood levels and outcomes; the fatal toxicity index (deaths per million defined daily doses) from a Finnish database.
outcomes.validity_norms: Information was missing for 177 of 330 ICD-10 items (54%) in the case reports: 122 of 216 for gabapentin (56%) and 55 of 114 for pregabalin (48%); the authors judge it more likely that a missing criterion was absent than present but unreported (PDF p. 13, 3.3, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Genuine' addictive power is taken to be behavioural dependence in people with no prior history of other substance use (apart from nicotine); severity is the number of fulfilled criteria; the other markers are transitions from prescribed doses to self-administration, duration, relapse, treatment seeking, social harm and overdose toxicity (PDF p. 3, 2.2).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Both authors reviewed titles and abstracts independently and agreed by consensus on full texts; disagreements were resolved by discussion (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 3rd paragraph). Who scored the case reports against ICD-10 criteria is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling; counts and proportions from the reviewers' tabulation of case reports and from the included studies. Case reports: tolerance or withdrawal 27/36 (75%) gabapentin and 16/19 (84%) pregabalin; behavioural dependence 3/36 (8%) and 15/19 (79%); three or more criteria 5/36 (14%) and 13/19 (68%); transition from prescription to self-administration 10/36 (28%) and 16/19 (84%); 4 cases, all pregabalin, with behavioural dependence and no other substance use history. Non-medical use in opioid-treatment populations: up-to-6-month prevalence 15–22% for gabapentin and 3–26% for pregabalin. General population: lifetime misuse of gabapentin 1.1% and pregabalin 0.5% (online survey, n=1500); lifetime gabapentinoid dependence 0.25% (one person, hospital survey of 400 people aged 65 or more). US poison-centre fatality records with a gabapentinoid: 1.5% (2012) to 4.3% (2015); gabapentinoid alone 0.05–0.07%. Fatal toxicity index: pregabalin 1.92, gabapentin 0.91 deaths per million defined daily doses.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned; PRISMA cited (PDF p. 3, 2.1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Case-report counts in the text do not always match the cases they cite (reporting issues), and the text's naming of the four abuse-history-free patients conflicts with Table 2. The authors' framework counts only what case reports state, then assumes unstated criteria were absent.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Weak or no rewarding effects of gabapentinoids in animal and laboratory studies; frequent non-medical use (up to about a quarter) in people in opioid treatment, all of whom were dependent on other substances; in published case reports, behavioural dependence far more often with pregabalin (15 of 19) than gabapentin (3 of 36), and only 4 cases (all pregabalin) without another substance use history; low lifetime figures in one online survey (gabapentin 1.1%, pregabalin 0.5% misuse) and one hospital survey of older people (0.25% dependence); rising numbers of deaths involving gabapentinoids, nearly always with opioids or other sedatives, and very few attributed to a gabapentinoid alone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract finds no convincing evidence of a strong addictive power, and the conclusion states that in patients without another substance use disorder "the risk to develop a dependence on gabapentinoids is very low" (PDF p. 26). Gaps: (1) the low risk is inferred from counts of case reports, which have no denominator, and from one survey of older hospital patients; comparing the 4 cases with the number of published cases of a rare syndrome (gut fermentation, PDF p. 26) cannot estimate frequency; (2) the 54% of ICD-10 items not reported in case descriptions are assumed absent (PDF p. 13), which biases the count of criteria downwards; (3) the star ratings in Table 4 are partly the authors' clinical opinion (PDF p. 25), and gabapentinoids are called certainly the safest GABA-mimetic drugs (PDF p. 23) without comparative data in the review; (4) the falling total of US poison-centre fatality records is offered as a possible sign that gabapentinoids replace more toxic drugs (PDF p. 24), although Table 3 describes the later reports as adult records; (5) the opioid-overdose evidence is summarized as gabapentinoids being relatively safe alone but able to become lethal in mixtures, while the register study with hazard ratios for overdose death (Abrahamsson et al., 2017) is listed without them. Balancing points: the authors say large registers cannot verify causal relationships (PDF p. 23), label their substitution idea as speculation (PDF p. 24), recommend avoiding or closely monitoring gabapentinoids in people with substance use disorders, and call for prospective studies (PDF p. 26).

timeline.event: Finnish post-mortem toxicology database study cited in Table 3 for gabapentin and pregabalin deaths; the project's card for it gives different figures from this review's (reporting issue)

Cossmann, Scherbaum and Bonnet, GeroPsych 29(1):17–27: the authors' own cross-sectional study of 400 inpatients aged 65 or more, the review's only hospital-population dependence figure (no project record).
Evoy, Morrison and Saklad, Drugs 77:403–426: a systematic review of gabapentinoid abuse published the same year and cited here (no project record).
Gomes et al.: prescribed gabapentin with opioids associated with opioid-related death (published after this review's search)
Gomes et al.: prescribed pregabalin with opioids associated with opioid-related death
Evoy et al.: systematic review update (to August 2020), which cites this review
The same authors' letter criticizing the update's causal conclusions, citing this review for the substitution hypothesis

replication.where_it_stands: Still the most detailed appraisal in the files read of the dependence criteria described in published gabapentinoid case reports, and the source of the only general-population figures in those files (one online survey, one hospital survey of older people). Its picture of overdose risk predates the case-control studies linking prescribed gabapentin and pregabalin taken with opioids to opioid-related death (Gomes et al., 2017, 2018). The German detoxification sample it cites as Snellgrove (2016) appears as Snellgrove et al. (2017) in Evoy et al. (2021) with a different dependence figure (11%); the primary paper should be read before either is cited.

funding.funder: Role of the funding source: None (PDF p. 26).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of interest: None to declare (PDF p. 26).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Psychotherapy and Psychosomatic Medicine, Evangelisches Krankenhaus Castrop-Rauxel (academic teaching hospital of the University of Duisburg-Essen), and Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, LVR-Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen (PDF p. 1). Two included sources are the authors' own (Cossmann et al., 2016; Bonnet and Scherbaum, 2016), and the ratings in Table 4 for the traditional drugs draw partly on the authors' expertise in treating addiction (PDF p. 25). In their 2021 letter on the same subject, Scherbaum declared honoraria from several pharmaceutical companies (sc_bonnet_2021); none is declared here. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies, as the authors propose, comparing the frequency and pattern of dependence criteria and drug safety during gabapentinoid treatment in patients with and without another substance use disorder; and population surveys that measure non-medical gabapentinoid use and DSM-5 use disorder with denominators of people exposed.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Drugs, outcome domains (reward, dependence, overdose) and eligible study types are specified (PDF p. 3, 2.1–2.2); the question is descriptive, with Table 4 as a qualitative comparison.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Animal, laboratory, clinical, case-report and overdose evidence are included as successive steps of a stated framework for judging addiction risk (PDF p. 3, 2.2, A to F).

Two databases with the search terms and dates given, reference lists hand-searched, no language restriction stated, search to March 2017 for a 2017 paper; but no trial or study registries, no grey-literature search beyond agency reports, and no experts consulted.
Both authors reviewed the records independently, agreed by consensus on full texts and resolved disagreements by discussion (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 3rd paragraph).
Not described; who scored the case reports against ICD-10 criteria is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only grouped reasons for the 63 full-text exclusions (Figure 1, PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1 to 3 give population, methods, results, addiction history and (for Table 3) limitations; Table 2 scores each case against the ICD-10 criteria. Sample sizes are missing for some studies (for example the volunteer study of Zacny et al.), and how non-medical use was defined in each study is not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool. Table 3 has a limitations column; the clinical studies in Table 1 are not appraised for confounding or selection, and case reports are not appraised.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Some limits are discussed (registers cannot verify causality; missing ICD-10 items), but the missing items are then assumed absent and the conclusion that dependence risk is very low in people without substance use disorders is drawn from case-report counts without discussing the absence of denominators or publication selection (PDF pp. 13, 23, 26).

Differences in prevalence are discussed in terms of population (opioid substitution and prescription-opioid cohorts against general and hospital populations; the Swiss study finding none) and drug (pregabalin against gabapentin) (PDF pp. 13, 22).
No pooling; publication selection of case reports is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (PDF p. 26); the inclusion of two of the authors' own studies is not flagged.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, no protocol; 7, no list of excluded studies; 9, no appraisal of included studies; 13, risk of bias not carried into the conclusion) and one only partly (4), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The review's search and selection were done reasonably for its time, and its tabulation of case reports by ICD-10 criteria is useful and transparent; its weakness is the inference from case counts to population risk. Cite it for what the case literature to March 2017 described (which drug, which criteria, which histories), for the rates it tabulates in opioid-treatment samples, and as a pointer to fatality sources; do not cite its 'very low risk' conclusion or Table 4 as measured findings.

key_findings.finding: PubMed and Scopus were searched from market introduction (gabapentin 1997, pregabalin 2004) to 31 March 2017, with a hand search of reference lists: 1073 database and 19 hand-search records, 878 screened, 169 full texts, 106 included (17 on rewarding effects, 14 clinical studies, 38 case-report publications, 37 overdose and fatality publications).
key_findings.note: The counts other than 106 are printed only in Figure 1, which has no text layer; read on the rendered page (legible).

key_findings.finding: Rewarding effects (17 publications): gabapentin at doses assumed to be therapeutic did not produce place preference in rodents, and pregabalin did so only at a higher injected dose; no animal study of gabapentin self-administration alone was found; in rhesus monkeys trained to self-administer barbiturates, pregabalin was not reinforcing in one set of experiments and weakly reinforcing at two doses in another, an effect that faded within the first week; gabapentin did not change cocaine self-administration in rats or in three studies of people who used cocaine; in healthy volunteers, pregabalin 75 mg and 150 mg did not change liking or desire to take the drug. The authors conclude gabapentin has no relevant rewarding properties and pregabalin low ones, only at doses assumed to be above the therapeutic range.

Non-medical use in opioid-treatment populations, up-to-6-month prevalence 15–22% for gabapentin and 3–26% for pregabalin. Examples from Table 1: Scottish detoxification clinics (n=129), gabapentin 19% and pregabalin 3%, all of them in opioid substitution; Irish opioid substitution (n=440), pregabalin in urine without medical purpose 7%; US inpatients detoxifying from opioids (n=162), gabapentin misuse 22% and pregabalin 7%; US former prisoners (n=250), gabapentin misuse 16% overall, 26% of those with opioid use disorder (n=145) against 4% without (n=105); German opioid substitution (n=124), non-medical pregabalin 12.1%, against 2.7% positive among 111 people treated for other addictions, all of whom had a prescription; Kentucky (n=503 people using prescription opioids non-medically), non-medical gabapentin use in 6 months 15%; Georgia (n=506), pregabalin 8.17%; Finnish methadone programme, 200 urine samples, gabapentin 0.5% and pregabalin 4%; Swiss methadone programme (n=109), none.

General population: the review states that no epidemiological survey had measured gabapentinoid abuse or dependence in the general population, and gives two rough estimates: an online survey of 1500 people aged 16–59 in England and Wales (Kapil et al., 2014) with lifetime misuse of gabapentin 1.1% (17 people) and pregabalin 0.5% (8) (baclofen 1.3%, 19); and the authors' own structured-interview study (SKID-I) of 400 inpatients aged 65 or more in a German general hospital in 2013 (Cossmann et al., 2016) with lifetime gabapentinoid dependence 0.25% (one man with transient gabapentin dependence, who was also dependent on an opioid pain reliever), 12-month prevalence 0%, and no case with pregabalin.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Internet and hospital population (PDF p. 5); 4.2, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 22)
key_findings.note: The text of 3.2 calls the 0.25% a 12-month prevalence (PDF p. 4; reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: German qualified-detoxification ward (Snellgrove, 2016; n=253, all dependent on other substances, mostly opioids or benzodiazepines): pregabalin use in the last 30 days 26% (65) and lifetime 56% (142); pregabalin dependence point prevalence 3% and 24-month prevalence 7%; 13% of those with non-medical pregabalin use had met three DSM-IV dependence criteria for more than 12 months, and 6% of 'this cohort' (apparently those with non-medical use, as Table 1 gives a point prevalence of 3% for all patients) were dependent at interview; 9% of those with pregabalin experience had used it on 25 or more days a month for 12 months; sources were family or acquaintances for free (44%), dealers (41%) and physicians (30%).
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 4); Table 1, Snellgrove (2016) (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Evoy et al. (2021, Table 1, PDF p. 17) cite this sample (n=253) as Snellgrove et al. (2017) with 11% of those who used pregabalin meeting DSM-IV dependence criteria.

key_findings.finding: Case reports (36 gabapentin and 19 pregabalin case presentations): tolerance and withdrawal were common (27/36, 75%, and 16/19, 84%); behavioural dependence was far rarer with gabapentin (3/36, 8%) than pregabalin (15/19, 79%); three or more criteria in 5/36 (14%) and 13/19 (68%); transition from prescribed doses to self-administration in 10/36 (28%) and 16/19 (84%); self-administration for more than a year in no gabapentin and 3 pregabalin reports (2 to 4 years); relapse in 1 gabapentin and 2 pregabalin reports; only three cases met more than four of the six criteria (two pregabalin, one gabapentin).

Only 4 patients, all with pregabalin, showed behavioural dependence without a history of other substance use disorders apart from nicotine; the vast majority of cases with self-administration had a history of addiction to alcohol, benzodiazepines or opioids.
key_findings.note: The text names one of the four wrongly by Table 2's own entries (reporting issue); the count of 4 is consistent with Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Information was missing for 177 of 330 ICD-10 items (54%) in the case presentations (122 of 216, 56%, for gabapentin; 55 of 114, 48%, for pregabalin); the authors consider it more likely that a missing criterion was simply not present than present but not described.

Withdrawal: 25 of the 36 gabapentin case presentations concerned only withdrawal symptoms or rebound of psychiatric symptoms after stopping therapeutic gabapentin; the withdrawal described resembled benzodiazepine withdrawal (including seizures and delirium) or SSRI discontinuation, responded poorly to benzodiazepines, and improved after a gabapentinoid was restarted and tapered.
key_findings.note: The cases the text cites for the 25 add up to fewer patients (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: No report was found of anyone seeking treatment for gabapentinoid misuse or dependence, nor relevant information on social harm attributable to gabapentinoids alone; the review notes that gabapentinoids appeared to be used mostly together with other substances.
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 5th paragraph and 3.3, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 13); 4 Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 22)

key_findings.finding: Non-fatal overdoses: 9 gabapentin case presentations and one case series (20 pure gabapentin exposures reported to three poison centres, 9 with symptoms, none admitted); the highest gabapentin blood levels, 104.5 and 126.8 mg/L, came with coma, respiratory depression or cardiopulmonary resuscitation, both with other medicines taken; a single-drug pregabalin overdose caused coma and respiratory depression needing mechanical ventilation; a US poison-centre analysis of 94 gabapentin and 18 pregabalin overdoses found no severe outcome and no death.
key_findings.locator: 3.4, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 21); Table 3, Klein-Schwartz et al. (2003) (PDF p. 14) and Wills et al. (2014) (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Breathing in healthy volunteers (Zacny et al., 2012; randomized, double-blind, crossover): respiration rate with placebo 12.9 against 10.3 with pregabalin 75 mg, 10.6 with pregabalin 150 mg, 10.5 with oxycodone 10 mg and 9.6 with oxycodone 10 mg plus pregabalin 75 mg; a planned condition combining pregabalin 150 mg with oxycodone 10 mg was not studied further because two participants reported excessive drowsiness. The review's text calls the reduction with pregabalin slight.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Zacny et al. (2012) (PDF p. 15); 3.4, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 21)
key_findings.note: Values as printed with ± 0.5 to 0.8 (SD or SE not stated) and no units; the number of volunteers is not given (15 reported cannabis use). Doses are the study's conditions.

key_findings.finding: Seizures: of 10 young adults seen at a Belfast emergency department after recreational pregabalin use (Millar et al., 2013), 6 (60%) had seizures, 5 of them first seizures, and 2 (20%) needed intubation, ventilation and intensive care.

Deaths: of 19 publications on fatalities, 9 register studies (Finland, Sweden, Germany, the UK and European pharmacovigilance) all point to increasing deaths involving gabapentinoids (mainly pregabalin) over 15 years, nearly always with other drugs, mostly opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants; the review counts 6 detailed post-mortem case reports with gabapentin and 35 with pregabalin as the main cause of death; suicide with pregabalin alone had not been described.
key_findings.note: The 35 cannot be reconciled with the sources cited (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: US poison-centre annual reports: fatality records involving a gabapentinoid were 38 of 2576 (1.5%) in 2012, 41 of 2113 (1.9%) in 2013, 41 of 1408 (2.9%) in 2014 and 59 of 1371 (4.3%) in 2015; pregabalin-involved deaths (7, 7, 11, 8) always involved other medicines; in each of 2013 to 2015 one record (0.05–0.07% of all fatality records) was attributed to a gabapentinoid alone, always gabapentin.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Mowry et al. (2013 to 2016) (PDF pp. 19–20); 3.4, 5th paragraph (PDF pp. 21–22)

key_findings.finding: Finnish fatal toxicity index (deaths per million defined daily doses; Ojanperä et al., 2016): pregabalin 1.92 (rising from 0.54 in 2005 to 1.54 in 2009 and 2.44 in 2013) and gabapentin 0.91, in the middle of 70 ranked medicines (for example methadone 42.65, tramadol 5.69, quetiapine 2.51); pregabalin was involved in 39 (0.2%) and gabapentin in 6 (0.03%) of 19,670 drug-related deaths.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Ojanperä et al. (2016) (PDF p. 17); 3.4, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 21)

key_findings.finding: Finnish autopsy database 2000–2010 (Launiainen and Ojanperä, 2014): gabapentin was involved in 135 (0.23%) and pregabalin in 380 (0.66%) of 57,903 cases; the review reports 8 of 135 (6%) and 12 of 380 (3.2%) as the drug being the main cause of death on death certificates.
key_findings.note: The project's card for the primary paper gives these as percentages (8% and 12%) of cases certified as poisoning by the drug (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Pharmacovigilance (EudraVigilance, 2004–2015): misuse reports for gabapentin (4301 records, 410 patients) and pregabalin (7639 records, 1315 patients); gabapentin fatality reports 86 (21%), with no other drug reported in 3 (3.5%); pregabalin fatality reports 27 (2%), with no other drug reported in 5 (18.5%). The authors note that most registered patients were dependent on other substances and that gabapentinoids may be bystanders of other substance use disorders.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 2); Table 3, Chiappini and Schifano (2016) (PDF p. 18)

key_findings.finding: England and Wales (Office for National Statistics): deaths related to drug poisoning that mention gabapentin rose from 4 (2011) to 49 (2015) and pregabalin from 4 to 90, against all drug-poisoning deaths of 2652 and 3674; over half of the deaths involved an opioid. The authors caution that death certificates often name several drugs or none specifically, so the register shows trends but not which drug caused a death.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Office for National Statistics (2016) (PDF pp. 18–19); 4.4, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 23)

key_findings.finding: Finnish medico-legal deaths 2010–2011 (Häkkinen et al., 2014): among 316 pregabalin and 43 gabapentin cases, a history of drug abuse was recorded in 48.1% and 18.6%, and of those with such a history 91.4 and 87.5 (percent signs missing in the table) had also used opioids.

Why people with other substance use prefer pregabalin, as the authors explain it: faster absorption (peak blood level within 1.5 hours), higher oral bioavailability (above 90% against 33–66% for gabapentin), absorption proportional to dose (gabapentin's is saturable), and stronger binding at the α2δ target, giving a faster and stronger high.

Table 4 (the authors' comparative ratings, from very weak to very strong): overdose toxicity gabapentin very weak and pregabalin weak, against strong for benzodiazepines and very strong for opioids; physical dependence moderate for both gabapentinoids, strong for benzodiazepines; behavioural dependence rated very weak in brackets for gabapentin, only in people with a history of substance use disorder, and very weak for pregabalin, especially in such people; voluntary treatment seeking none for either. Ratings for gabapentinoids are based on this review; those for the traditional drugs on other reviews and the authors' expertise in treating addiction.

The authors speculate (and say further research is needed) that gabapentinoids might replace more toxic benzodiazepines among people who use opioids and other drugs, reducing deaths (an 'anti-adverse selection' process), and name the opposite view that gabapentinoids open a Pandora's box in people with substance use histories.

Conclusion: the addiction risk of gabapentin is lower than that of pregabalin and depends on the population exposed; in patients without a current or past substance use disorder the risk of dependence is called very low and treatment can be managed like other common medicines; in patients with a history of substance use disorder, especially opioid use disorder, gabapentinoids (notably pregabalin) should be avoided or, if indispensable, given under strict therapeutic and prescription monitoring; prospective studies comparing patients with and without substance use disorders are missing.

reporting_issues.issue: The text names the four abuse-history-free patients with behavioural dependence as Yargic and Ozdemiroglu (2011), Ashwini et al. (2015), Halaby et al. (2015) and Driot et al. (2016) (3.3; 4 Discussion; 4.6), but Table 2 gives Yargic and Ozdemiroglu's patient a history of benzodiazepine and ketamine use, while Westin and Strøm (2010), not named, is the pregabalin case in Table 2 with a negative history and a behavioural criterion (loss of control) fulfilled.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of four stands, but one named case is wrong by the review's own table; a claim citing the four cases should take them from Table 2 (Westin and Strøm, Ashwini, Halaby, Driot).

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says Cossmann et al. (2016) found a 12-month prevalence of gabapentinoid dependence of 0.25%; Table 1 gives a 12-month prevalence of 0% and a lifetime prevalence of 0.25% (one transient case), and the Discussion (4.2) uses 0.25% as lifetime prevalence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0.25% is lifetime, one person in 400 older inpatients; no current dependence was found. The same authors' 2021 letter gives different counts for what appears to be the same sample (see sc_bonnet_2021).

reporting_issues.issue: For the Finnish autopsy database (Launiainen and Ojanperä, 2014), Table 3 reports 8 of 135 gabapentin records (6%) and 12 of 380 pregabalin records (3.2%) as the drug being the main cause of death. The project's card for the primary paper (sc_launiainen_2014, ai-checked, from its Table 2) gives the share of cases certified as poisoning by the drug as 8% for gabapentin (N=135) and 12% for pregabalin (N=380).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review appears to have read the percentages as counts; on the primary paper's figures about 11 gabapentin and 46 pregabalin deaths were certified as poisoning by the drug (editors' arithmetic: 8% of 135; 12% of 380), so the review understates them. Check at the source before citing either version.

reporting_issues.issue: The review counts 35 detailed post-mortem case reports with pregabalin as the main cause of death (3.4), but the six sources it cites for them, as Table 3 describes them, account for 22: Button et al. 2, Priez-Barallon et al. 3, Häkkinen et al. 2, Eastwood and Davison 1, Chiappini and Schifano 5 (no other drug reported) and Elliott et al. 9 (editors' count). The 6 gabapentin cases do match their sources (1 + 1 + 1 + 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that there are nearly six times more pregabalin than gabapentin main-cause reports rests on a number the tables do not support; and several of the cited pregabalin cases are described in Table 3 as involving other drugs or doubtful causality.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 says 25 of the 36 gabapentin cases concerned only withdrawal or rebound after stopping therapeutic use and the remaining 11 had taken markedly higher doses than prescribed, but the cases it cites for the first group account for 20 patients according to the descriptions in Table 2 (21 with Di Fabio et al., 2013, described the same way in Table 2 but not named), and those cited for the second group for 15 (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The split of gabapentin cases between withdrawal after prescribed use and self-administration at higher doses is about 21 to 15, not 25 to 11; it does not change the overall conclusion but shows the counts should be taken from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The rise in the share of US poison-centre fatality records involving gabapentinoids, from 1.5% (2012) to 4.3% (2015), is driven partly by a falling denominator (2576 to 1371 records), and Table 3 describes the 2014 and 2015 reports as registers of adult records but the 2012 and 2013 reports without that restriction; the falling total is also offered as a possible sign that gabapentinoids replace more toxic drugs (4.5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The absolute counts (38 to 59) are the safer figures; the percentage trend and the substitution signal may reflect a change in what the reports listed rather than in deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean fatal toxicity index of pregabalin is given as 1.92, but by the editors' arithmetic the three yearly values printed (0.54, 1.54 and 2.44) have a mean of 1.51; how the mean was calculated is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a pooled index rather than an average of the three years; cite the primary paper (Ojanperä et al., 2016) for the value.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller inconsistencies: citation years differ between text and tables or references (Aldemir et al. 2013 in the text, 2015 in Table 2 and the references; See et al. 2013 against 2011; Mutschler et al. 2015 against 2016; Launiainen et al. 2013 against 2014; Schauer et al. 2015 against 2013; Elliott et al. 2016 against 2017); case reports in Table 2 are cited as Table 1 (PDF pp. 13, 26); the text gives Miljevic et al.'s patient as 59 years old, Table 3 as 54; 'Kapril' for Kapil; Table 1 lists one Scottish result (N=61, 47%) without a drug name; the 13% of the Snellgrove sample is described as meeting three criteria for longer than 12 months (3.2) and as dependent for no longer than 2 years (4.3); and 3.2 summarizes the highest rates as up to every third or fourth patient, while Table 1's highest figures in opioid-treatment cohorts are 22–26%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor individually; together they mean figures and citations should be taken from the tables and the reference list, and checked against primary papers.
